scope_notes: Pearl Definition 1 (d-separation, p. 106) and its illustrations (path blocking on the chain, Berkson's paradox, the two-coin example, the remark that d-separation implications are the main opening for testing, note 7) were treated as the extent of the graphical-separation chapter, which cites Definition 1 p. 106, and were not counted against these components. The sec. 3 introduction above sec. 3.1 on p. 103 was treated as outside the cited sections.

Lauritzen p. 68: only its opening remark (a structural-equation network need not have a density with respect to any product measure; covered by thm:p16-measurable-graph-examples and body 10-12) was counted; (F), Proposition 2.51, Lemma 2.52 and Theorem 2.53 are not among the locator's named results.

Lauritzen Definition 2.47 calls the recursive combination a Bayesian network; def:p16-measurable-dag-kernels defines the same object as a kernel model. The p. 65 lead-in contrast with the undirected case is preserved in substance (only S1-S4; no intersection, positivity or probability: body 209-211).
Lauritzen Theorem 1.28 is preserved in kernel form for every parameter; the joint-law transfer for an independent uniform is written in the whole-model paragraph (annex 276-312).

components.gap: ED26-P16-CH-finite-causal-models-C003 (partial): preserve the source's path-analysis paragraph (Pearl 2009, sec. 3.1, p. 105): (i) the historical claim that Wright's major contribution, aside from introducing the language of path diagrams, was the development of graphical rules for writing down the covariance of any pair of observed variables in terms of path coefficients and of covariances among the error terms, of which (3) and (4) are the instances for Fig. 1; (ii) the remark that these relations can be derived from the equations, but that for large models algebraic methods tend to obscure the origin of the derived quantities; (iii) the claim that under certain conditions (e.g. Cov(U_Y,U_X)=0) such relations allow the path coefficients to be solved in terms of observed covariance terms only, which amounts to inferring the magnitude of (direct) causal effects from observed, nonexperimental associations, provided one is prepared to defend the causal assumptions encoded in the diagram. parts/p16/finite-causal-models.tex 89-143 and 164-185 reproduce the surrounding sentences and give (3)-(4) only as consequences of the algebraic thm:p15-w02c-p15-009-linear-effect (818-860); (i) and (ii) are absent from the route, and for (iii) the route states only that beta is identified under the missing links (168-172) and that the least-squares slope equals beta exactly when Cov(X,U_Y)=0 (838-841), not the source's conclusion with its proviso.

components.gap: ED26-P16-CH-finite-causal-models-C012 (partial): preserve the source's p. 106 treatment of its chain (Fig. 2(a), Pearl 2009, sec. 3.1): the chain model encodes seven causal assumptions, each corresponding to a missing arrow or a missing double arrow between a pair of variables; none of them is testable in isolation; yet their totality implies that Z is unassociated with Y in every stratum of X, the source's example that the sum total of a model's causal assumptions often has testable implications.
